calls.transcript:
Alex (NexusStream): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I see the audio connecting... Marcus, good to speak with you again. And Jennifer, really nice to meet you.

Jennifer Wu: Hi Alex. Nice to meet you too.

Marcus Thorne: Hey Alex. Yeah, we're both here. Sorry we're a minute late, just coming out of a—well, another fireside chat about logistics, ironically.

Alex: No worries at all. I know you guys are coming off that heavy Quarterly Ops Review week, so I appreciate the time. How did things shake out, if you don't mind me asking? Hopefully the dust has settled a bit?

Marcus Thorne: [Laughs] The dust never really settles here, Alex. But yeah, we survived. It actually highlighted exactly why we're talking today. The numbers... look, the numbers on the North Atlantic lanes were pretty brutal in Q4.

Alex: Yeah, you mentioned the margin compression on the phone Friday. I want to dig into that, but before we do—Jennifer, Marcus gave me the heads up that you’re the one keeping the ship afloat technically. I know the SAP migration recently was... let's call it a heavy lift.

Jennifer Wu: That is the understatement of the year. Look, Alex, I'll be straight with you because I have a hard stop at the top of the hour. We spent eight months integrating SAP S/4HANA. It was a nightmare. My team is burnt out. We are currently in a 'stabilization period' mandated by the CIO. So, when Marcus tells me we need another software tool, my immediate answer is 'no' if it requires heavy lifting, agents on servers, or complex middleware. So, I'm here to see if 'easy integration' is just sales talk or reality.

Alex: I appreciate the candor, Jennifer. Truly. And to set the stage: if this requires a consulting team or more than 10 hours of your team's time to deploy, we aren't the right fit. We built NexusStream specifically as a lightweight API overlay for this exact reason. We pull, we don't push, and we don't alter your ERP data structures.

Jennifer Wu: Okay. That's... refreshing to hear, at least. We can get into the weeds later, but keep going.

Alex: Great. So, agenda for today: I want to understand the specific bottlenecks hitting those margins, map out what your current stack looks like—specifically how you're handling route forecasting now—and then if it makes sense, we can discuss a technical proof of concept. Sound fair?

Marcus Thorne: Sounds good.

Alex: Marcus, back to that Q4 performance. You mentioned the North Atlantic routes. Walk me through what happened there.

Marcus Thorne: Right. So, fuel costs spiked—everyone knows that. But our issue was the BAF—the Bunker Adjustment Factor. We were calculating it based on historical data from Q3. By the time our ships hit the water in November, the port congestion in Hamburg caused idle times to triple. We burned way more fuel sitting at anchor than we accounted for. We couldn't pass those costs on to the customers because the quotes were already locked.

Alex: Ouch. So the latency in data cost you the margin.

Marcus Thorne: Exactly. It’s the lag. We're driving looking in the rearview mirror.

Alex: Do you have a sense of the financial impact of that specific lag in Q4?

Marcus Thorne: I pulled the report this morning. Just on unrecovered fuel surcharges due to port delays? We took a $1.2 million hit. And that's just one quarter.

Alex: Wow. Okay, $1.2 million. That’s... significant. And how are you tracking these bottlenecks right now? What's the workflow?

Marcus Thorne: It's manual. Too manual. We get reports from the carriers, usually via email or EDI, but they're delayed. Then my analysts dump that into Excel.

Jennifer Wu: Well, it's not just Excel, Marcus. We are pulling data into 'RouteMaster.'

Alex: RouteMaster? I haven't seen them in a while. Is that the on-prem version or cloud?

Jennifer Wu: It's legacy on-prem. It’s clunky. It doesn't talk to SAP well, which is why the analysts are dumping data to CSVs and then re-uploading. It's a mess. That's where the 'Integration Fatigue' comes from. Connecting RouteMaster to SAP took us three months and it still breaks.

Alex: Got it. So you have SAP as the source of truth for financials, RouteMaster for—theoretically—routing, but the bridge is broken, and neither is giving you predictive fuel burn data.

Jennifer Wu: Correct. And RouteMaster doesn't do ML. It just shows us where the ship is. It doesn't tell us 'Hey, Hamburg is backed up 4 days, re-route to Rotterdam.'

Alex: Okay. That’s the gap. So, if NexusStream could ingest that manifest data from SAP via API, run it against our port congestion models, and push an alert back saying 'Predicted delay 48 hours, estimated fuel cost +$15k'—before the ship leaves—that solves the visibility issue?

Marcus Thorne: If you can do that in real-time? Yeah. That changes the game. We can adjust the quote or re-route.

Jennifer Wu: The functionality sounds fine, but let's talk security. If you're pulling data via API, are you SOC 2 Type II compliant? And what’s the API call limit? We have high transaction volumes.

Alex: We are SOC 2 Type II compliant, I can send the package over right after this call. As for limits, we scale automatically. We handle high-frequency trading logistics for some enterprise clients, so volume won't be an issue. We use a RESTful API, standard JSON payload. Do you have a sandbox environment for SAP?

Jennifer Wu: We do. A staging environment.

Alex: Ideally, we’d connect to that first. We usually see a 'Hello World' connection established in under an hour.

Jennifer Wu: [Sighs] Okay. If you can send me the API documentation and the security whitepaper, I’ll take a look tonight. If it's as standard as you say, I might be open to a sandbox test.

Alex: I’ll get that to you within 15 minutes. Marcus, looking at the calendar, we’re heading into peak season prep in a few months. What’s your timeline for fixing this leak?

Marcus Thorne: We can't take another hit like Q4. We need to be running differently by August. So, Q3 go-live is the goal.

Alex: Understood. If Jennifer gives the green light on the technical side, typically we run a 2-week proof of value using historical data. We take that Q4 data you lost money on, run it through our model, and show you what we *would* have predicted. 

Marcus Thorne: I’d like to see that. If you can prove you would have caught that Hamburg delay, I can get the budget approved. The CFO is already breathing down my neck about the fuel costs.

Alex: Perfect. Let's target that. Jennifer, I'll send the docs. Marcus, I'll send a summary of what we discussed. Shall we tentatively hold this time next Tuesday to review the API docs and maybe look at that historical data?

Jennifer Wu: Send the docs first. If they look like spaghetti code, I'm cancelling.

Alex: [Laughs] Fair enough, Jennifer. Challenge accepted. Thanks for the time, folks.

Marcus Thorne: Thanks Alex.
